content_preview.title: Disclosure Rules Shift Around AI-Found Bugs: Kernel Docs Say Treat Them as Public, GNOME Ended Its Bounty, Google Paused OSS Rewards
content_preview.summary: Kernel docs, GNOME, Google, Go and PHP each handled AI-found vulnerabilities differently in October, from report volume to CVE assignment and embargo timing.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Background

The Linux kernel's published security-bug guidance shows how the usual order of private report, embargoed fix and CVE identifier is being restated for bugs found with AI tools. [The kernel document](https://docs.kernel.org/process/security-bugs.html) says that a reporter who resorted to AI assistance to identify a bug "must treat it as public", because the security team's experience is that bugs discovered this way "systematically surface simultaneously across multiple researchers...

editor_notes.content_quality: Qualifies as Analysis. 1,411 words (link URLs stripped; range 800-2000). Structure is Background, Current situation (Volume then Timing), Implications, What is not known. It examines a cross-project theme (report volume and embargo timing under AI-assisted bug finding) rather than recapping a release. Implications are labelled as what the sources imply, not forecasts; the Register column is explicitly labelled the column's opinion. Internal links (Google pause, curl 8.23.0, PHP release, Ruby/GitLab) all resolve to published articles and are described consistently (Google pause: product rewards stopped, update promised Q1 2027; Ruby: project had not requested CVE IDs for regexp bugs behind four GitLab CVEs).
editor_notes.source_verification: All 10 snapshots read from disk (source-0..9.html.gz); no suspicious_patterns in any manifest entry. INDEPENDENT-SOURCE COUNT: 3 independent outlets / 7 independent URLs (The Hacker News x2, The Register x4, BleepingComputer x1); requirement of at least 2 independent is met. Not counted as independent: docs.kernel.org (project's own docs), Catanzaro's GNOME blog (GNOME developer, the subject), go.dev (Go's own policy). Allowlist: docs.kernel.org, blogs.gnome.org, go.dev, thehackernews.com, theregister.com, bleepingcomputer.com are all already listed exactly; no edits. BleepingComputer: the live fetch was bot-blocked and chief:review used an Archive.org capture (source-9, archive_fallback true, HTTP 200, Wayback capture 2026-10-25) which is raw page text; the claims rest on it were verified there directly: the PHP team's quote 'We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild', watchTowr's leak warning, the now-deleted Hacker News post by a user naming both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, PHP advisory on Tuesday for a Wednesday October 21 release. TITLE CLAIMS: (1) 'Kernel Docs Say Treat Them as Public' - source-0 (security-bugs.rst rendered at docs.kernel.org) says verbatim 'If you resorted to AI assistance to identify a bug, you must treat it as public', with 'bugs discovered this way systematically surface simultaneously across multiple researchers, often on the same day'; 'significant fraction', 'forced to ignore such reports due to their poor quality or accuracy', 7 calendar days extendable to 14, and 'The security team does not assign CVEs' all verbatim. Accurate. (2) 'GNOME Ended Its Bounty' - source-1: the GNOME Bug Bounty Program on YesWeHack; Catanzaro writes 'I requested that the bug bounty program end because I was overwhelmed with incoming AI-generated issue reports'; the final issue was reported February 23, 2026, and the post (October 2) announces the end after the last bounty was awarded. 298 submitted / 71 accepted / 30 duplicates / 197 rejected confirmed. Accurate, but the article does not say the program closed in February (see correction 1). (3) 'Google Paused OSS Rewards' - source-3 (THN, Oct 6): Open Source Software Vulnerability Reward Program stopped accepting product vulnerability reports from October 1; Google called the stop temporary in an X post; quote 'a significant rise in automated submissions, the vast majority of which are not valid' verbatim; THN states the post gave no figures and did not say whether AI tools produced them; update promised Q1 2027; supply chain compromise rewards continue. Accurate and the article carries THN's caveat. OTHER FIGURES: Debian DSA-6528-1 published September 29, 1,313 CVE identifiers, counted by The Register (source-5); 'We strongly suspect that this number of CVEs is due to LLM bots' and the caveat about older kernels both verbatim and attributed to the outlet; kernel CNA since February 2024 and automatic assignment after stable fix confirmed. GNOME 90-to-30-day deadline effective August 1: source-6 (Register) says so, announced 'the following month' after a June post; accurate. Catanzaro CVE table: 2023 = 13; 2026 year-to-date (2026-09-30) = 141 as labelled in the table; 'AI is the primary cause for the increase' verbatim, but see correction 2. 'People will submit bad reports when financially incentivized', 'might as well ban all vulnerability reports', 'exist only because I request them myself', 'nobody else has volunteered', Apple/WebKit CVE statement, and resume-conditions all confirmed. Go policy (source-2): 'do not send LLM-generated reports without proper curation', 'only attribute discoveries to reporters with a substantial percentage of real findings', 'All security issues will be issued CVE numbers' verbatim. PHP/Chainguard (source-7, Register): PHP blog says CVE IDs circulated Tuesday ~15:00 UTC, release moved forward a day, Chainguard published built images at Oct 21 07:41 UTC 'more than six hours before the coordinated release' and 'unilaterally broke the embargo'; Lorenc says his company 'didn't leak', found the bugs independently with an AI harness and a frontier model, and quotes 'People were getting hit in advance' and 'coordinated vulnerability disclosure, unless there's evidence of active exploits in the wild' verbatim. Both accounts are attributed and the article states they conflict; no claim goes beyond them. KSMBD (source-4, THN): ZDI reports credited to TrendAI scanner, sent to public lists without patches; the Kroah-Hartman quote is verbatim and was a reply to the VMware GPU driver report (article correctly says 'a separate report in the same batch'); no CVE IDs; Jeon's Sept 30 commit credited to a different reporter confirmed. THN's 'appeared to follow' kernel guidance attribution is preserved. Register column (source-8, columnist Rupert Goodwins): 'Disclosure needs to be a discipline, not a protocol', minimum number of people, patch liaison role all confirmed; article labels it opinion.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No fabricated specifics found. The theme (AI-found bugs straining disclosure) is the sources' own attribution in each case: kernel doc, Catanzaro and the Register attribute to AI explicitly; Google's stated cause is 'automated submissions' and the article says plainly that Google did not say AI was involved. 'At least four distinct CVE arrangements (kernel, Go, GNOME, Ruby/GitLab)' is labelled the Herald's own count and is defensible (a fifth, Apple/WebKit, is also in Catanzaro's post). Two imprecisions are handled in the corrections record: the summary/title framing of events as October developments when some predate October, and the GNOME CVE count caveats.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral. Opinions (Register column, Catanzaro, Lorenc) are attributed; Implications section is framed as what the sources imply and contains no forecast of the Herald's own.
editor_notes.originality: Cross-project synthesis; does not duplicate the Google, curl, PHP or Ruby briefings, which are linked and cited for continuity only. No overlap with recent Analysis articles.
concerns: Summary says projects handled AI-found vulnerabilities differently 'in October', but the GNOME bounty closed after a February 23, 2026 final report (announced October 2), the kernel guidance was updated in May 2026 per The Hacker News, and the GNOME deadline change took effect August 1. The body gives the October 2 and August 1 dates but never states the February closure.

Catanzaro's GNOME CVE table is by year reported, accurate 'through roughly September 1' by his own note, and he says AI is not the only reason (maintainers also got better at flagging); the article quotes only 'primary cause'.
Source-9 (BleepingComputer) was read from an Archive.org capture, not live.
recommendations: Future Analysis submissions should date each development explicitly in the body, especially when the headline groups events that did not all occur in the reporting month.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Meets the Analysis requirements (1,411 words, 10 sources, 3 independent outlets, facts separated from attributed opinion, no prediction) and the headline claims check out against the primary texts. Two minor clarifications are filed as a corrections record; neither touches the headline claims. Featured candidacy: 2 - cross-project look at how AI-found vulnerabilities are straining disclosure, bounties and embargoes, relevant to a broad open-source and security audience
